newsitem.title: UK: Britain signs up for oil-spill compensation plan.
newsitem.headline: Britain signs up for oil-spill compensation plan.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday became the first country to sign an international multi-million pound dollar compensation scheme for maritime disasters, a British minister said.

The Hazardous and Noxious Substances (HNS) Convention will provide compensation for loss or damage resulting from pollution, fire or explosion threatened or caused by hazardous and noxious substances carried on sea-going ships.
The HNS was first drawn up last May by the International Maritime Organisation.

"This is an important step toward the introduction of a compensation regime which underlines our commitment to maintain, and where possible, to improve the safety of life at sea and the prevention of marine pollution," Lord Goschen, Minister for Shipping and Aviation said at a London signing ceremony.

The fund, which is based on the existing oil pollution compensation regime, would be a two-tier system. Compensation would initially be paid by shipowners, who would be required to maintain insurance to cover their strict liability for damage.
Additional compensation would be available, if needed, from an international compensation fund financed by contributions from receivers of cargoes of hazardous and noxious substances.

The government's move follows two major oil tanker accidents off the British coast in the past 18 months. In February, the Sea Empress ran aground off the coast of Wales, spilling about 70,000 tonnes of oil into the sea.

Compensation to local businesses and fishermen affected by the spill was was expected to be around 76 million pounds ($120 million), most of which would be paid by the British government from a fund financed by a tax on oil importers.
In January 1995, the Braer oil tanker ran aground off the north coast of Scotand, spilling 84,000 tonnes of crude oil.
That spill was mostly broken up in heavy weather, but damage to salmon fisheries had, by the end of 1995, resulted in claims of almost 50 million pounds.
